judge.rationale: Integrity holds: no clipped, overlapping or placeholder content, and every page carries real text (the p4 stat row -4pts / 38% / 61% even carries its source line). Legibility is acceptable — single-column body, obvious reading order, running head/footer with page numbers on pp.2-9. Coherence is broadly consistent (same accent rule under each H1, same footer 'Client Confidential / x of 9 / 8 September 2026'), which is why it clears level 3, though the text measure looks inconsistent — the executive-summary and situation blocks on pp.2-3 sit in a narrower inset column than the full-measure paragraphs on pp.5-6. It fails level 4 on density and evidence. Every section is one short block on its own page: p.5 'Option A' is a single paragraph over ~15% of the page, p.6 'Option B' two paragraphs, p.7 'Recommendation' three short paragraphs, p.8 four bullets, p.9 three lines plus a one-item notes list — each leaving 70-80% of the sheet blank. For an assessment built on a three-year share decline and a widening price gap there is not one chart or table in nine pages; the p.4 stat trio is the only quantitative visual, and the trend it summarises is never plotted. Several titles are labels rather than conclusions ('The situation', 'Recommendation', 'Next steps'), and p.1 leaves the title block stranded in the upper third of an otherwise empty cover. Genericness: the wording is clearly written to this brief (38% gap, under-40s at 61% of growth, the two named options), but the visual treatment — one blue rule, default body type, no chart, no table, no imagery — would render identically for any other subject.

Integrity holds: nothing is clipped, overset or left as placeholder — page 2's boxed 'Key takeaways' bullets, page 4's KPI row and page 5's 'Notes and sources' list all render complete, and the running header (section name right, doc title left) plus footer (Internal use only / x/5 / 8 September 2026) repeat identically on pages 2-5. Legibility and reading order are fine: single measure, dark text on white, one clear heading per page under a consistent blue rule and a small section number ('01'-'05'). Coherence is also met — the same accent colour, heading weight, indented-rule callout treatment (page 2 box, page 3 'These paths are not fully exclusive', page 4 source line) and left margin recur without drift.

Level 4 fails on two counts. First, units: page 4's three big figures read '-4', '38', '61' with no pts or % on the numerals themselves; only the small captions beneath ('Price gap vs. private label', 'Under-40 share of category growth') rescue them, and '38' next to '61' invites reading both as the same kind of quantity. Second, structure versus purpose: this is a two-option recommendation and page 3 ('Two paths, two different businesses') argues both options entirely in running prose — there is no comparison table or chart of volume/margin/share consequences anywhere in the document, despite the brief being built on three specific numbers. Nothing is charted at all. Density compounds it: pages 2, 3, 4 and 5 each stop between a third and half of the way down the page, so the whole argument floats in the top band of five near-empty sheets rather than being paced deliberately.

On genericness: the cover (eyebrow 'Marketing Director', title, one-line subtitle, date, 'Confidential — internal use only') and the section-per-page memo skeleton would be indistinguishable if the topic were IT procurement. The only brief-specific visual moment is the three-figure KPI band on page 4; nothing in the typography, colour or composition says heritage food brand or category share.

Integrity holds: no clipping, no overflow, no placeholder text — the running header ("Brand Repositioning Assessment" left, section name right), footer triad (Confidential — Client firm / page x / date) and the blue rule under each H1 repeat identically on pages 2–5, and the cover's rule-over-title lockup is consistent with them. Legibility is fine at document size, and reading order is unambiguous on every page. So levels 1–3 are met. Level 4 is where it stops. The page titles are section labels, not conclusions: page 2 says "The situation" when the page's actual finding is that the gap is structural, not promotional; page 3 says "The choice" when it concludes the two paths are not reversible in sequence; page 5 says "What would change this recommendation" and then buries the falsifier list in a single prose paragraph rather than as discrete testable conditions. Only page 4 carries an exhibit — the -4pts / 38% / 61% stat row, correctly unitised and sourced to "Client shopper panel and category tracking, 2026" — and it is the single piece of visual evidence in the whole document. A brief built on a three-year share slide and a widening price gap has no trend line, and a document whose entire job is to choose between two options has no side-by-side comparison of them; pages 2, 3 and 5 are unbroken prose with only the "Definition" box on page 3 and the two bullet lists as relief. Consequence: pages 2–5 all end around the 40–50% mark, leaving half of each page blank while the argument is compressed into paragraphs. Not shippable as-is — the analysis is there but it is undernourished visually, and the client would have to read the whole thing to extract what a comparison table would have shown at a glance. Genericness: the prose is specific to the brief (under-40 shoppers, 61% of category growth, matched-pack-size price gap), but the visual system — thin blue rule, small serif-free heads, stat row, definition box — is a neutral consultancy shell that would render identically for a telecom churn memo; nothing in the typography, colour or cover treatment signals a 90-year-old food brand or its heritage-versus-dated tension.

Integrity holds: no clipped, overlapping or placeholder content anywhere; the running header ("Cost Programme Review — Month 14" with section label right-aligned) and the footer ("Confidential — Internal / 1–5 / 8 September 2026") repeat identically on pages 2–5, the blue rule under each H1 is consistent, and page 4's stat row and page 5's "Notes and sources" list are properly formed. Legibility is acceptable for print-scale reading and the reading order is unambiguous. Coherence is met — the type ramp, the thin rule motif and the single blue accent (cover eyebrow "Transformation Office", H1 underline) agree on every page.

It fails at level 4 on density and structure. Pages 2, 3 and 5 place a single short text block in the top quarter of the page and leave the remaining ~70% blank; page 4 ends after the stat row and source line at roughly a third of the page. That is not deliberate white space — it is a five-page shell carrying about a page and a half of content, and nothing on any page anchors the lower two-thirds. Worse, the deliverable the brief asks for is not structured: the three decisions and their named owners (Chief Operating Officer, Chief Information Officer, Transformation Programme Sponsor) are buried inside one long justified paragraph on page 4 under "The recovery path", where owners, deadlines and euro values are impossible to scan. That belongs in a decision table with owner and date columns. Likewise the workstream performance (118% / 41% / 33%) appears only as three headline figures on page 4; there is no chart or table comparing banked EUR 19m against the EUR 28m plan or against the EUR 46m two-year target, so the central financial story is carried entirely by prose on page 2. Page 3's "On the numbers" callout is the only structural device in the whole document and appears once.

Genericness: titles are argumentative and brief-specific ("Why property and IT have stalled", "What if nothing changes"), which lifts it above pure boilerplate, but the visual system — cover with eyebrow, title, subtitle, date, confidentiality line; then heading, rule, paragraphs — would render identically for any internal briefing. Nothing in the composition is shaped by a cost programme.

Integrity holds: no clipped text, no placeholder strings, no overlaps. Page 3's bar chart sits inside its column with axis labels, legend and a figure caption; page 4's workstream table (Target/Actual €m) renders fully with a callout box beneath it. Page 5 ends with a numbered Notes and sources block rather than trailing whitespace, and the large empty lower area on page 5 is a legitimate end-of-document run-out, not a broken frame. Legibility is fine for A4 print: the €19.0m / 68% / €4.5m stat row on page 2 is the correct focal weight, body text is well-leaded, and the single blue accent (rule under the eyebrow, chart bar, heading rules) carries all colour load with strong contrast. Coherence is consistent: eyebrow-plus-rule masthead, running header with section label right-aligned, footer with confidential mark, page number and date repeats identically on pages 2-5; page 1's title block uses the same eyebrow-rule device. Communicatively it is strong for the brief — titles are conclusions, not labels ('The programme is behind plan, and the gap is fixable this quarter', 'Procurement is carrying workstreams that are not yet pulling their weight', 'Property and IT are blocked on three decisions, not on capacity', 'Three decisions this quarter, named and owned'); the chart has a takeaway line and a source; the decisions carry named owners, forums and dates; the closing paragraph states the €39-40m landing point if nothing changes. Level 5 is withheld for craft reasons: page 3's chart is a three-bar plot given a full column of vertical space with a redundant single-series legend and a y-axis to 125 that leaves the top quarter of the plot empty, so the page's visual centre is a weak object; page 4's table has no zebra or unit-in-header discipline matching the chart's polish; page 5 is a wall of five near-identical paragraphs where the three decisions deserved the same structured treatment (numbered, owner column) that the rest of the document earns. Genericness is moderate-low: the eyebrow rule, stat row and takeaways box are a recognisable house style rather than a default Word look, but the underlying skeleton — cover, key-takeaways box, one chart page, one table page, one prose page — would transfer unchanged to any programme review.

Integrity holds: no clipping, no placeholder text, the chart on p3 and the table on p4 both render fully, and the header/footer band (running title, section label left/right, 'Confidential', page x/7, date) repeats identically on pp2-7. Legibility is fine at report scale, though the caption/source lines under the p4 table and the p3 figure note are the smallest grey type in the document and are close to the floor. Coherence mostly holds — navy eyebrow, rule-under-heading, and one-idea-per-page structure are consistent — but the KPI treatment breaks: p2 sets three stats in a horizontal row with delta arrows (19.0€m ▼ -9.0, 118% ▲ +18, 37% ▼ -63), while p6 sets the same device as a vertical stack (33€m / 46€m / 13€m) with no deltas and much wider leading; the same component is doing two different things. Unit style also drifts, 'EUR 46m' in body copy versus '46€m' in the stat blocks. Level 4 fails on density and structure rather than content: p5 (three decisions and owners) ends about a quarter down the page, p6's three stacked stats occupy the top third, and p7 — the 'what the transformation office should do this quarter' page — is a single five-line paragraph plus a one-item 'Notes and sources' list, leaving roughly three-quarters of every page from 5 onward blank. The closing action page in particular does not restate the three decisions, owners or deadlines in scannable form, so the document's most important page is its emptiest. Where it is strong is titling and evidence discipline: 'Procurement is ahead of target', 'Property and IT are blocked, not behind', 'If nothing changes, the programme lands short' are conclusions, the p3 chart carries a figure caption, a takeaway and a PMO source, the p4 table carries a source note plus a callout defining 'blocked', and the p5 bullets name Group Property Director, Chief Information Officer and Programme Sponsor. The prose is clearly written for this brief; the visual kit — navy accent, eyebrow, rule, stat trio, grey callout — would fit any cost-programme review unchanged.

Integrity holds: no clipping, no placeholder text, no overlap. Type and contrast read fine at A4, and the running head/footer pair ("CSRD Readiness Assessment" / section tag; "Confidential — Committee Use Only", n/8, date) repeats identically on pages 2–8, with the same rule-under-title and the same left-aligned heading position. Pages 2–4 are genuinely well made: the 82/34/29/19 KPI band on p.2 is ruled top and bottom with labels under each figure and a source line beneath; the p.3 bar chart carries a concluding title ("Two-thirds of the inventory is already in reach; the gap concentrates in Scope 3"), a numbered figure caption, an axis label ("Datapoints (count)"), a legend stating "of 82" and a source; the p.4 ESRS pillar table has a stub column, a total-style gap column, a note line and a boxed Scope 3 definition. Where it fails is level 4, density and structure fit to purpose. Pages 5, 6, 7 and 8 each carry a heading plus one undifferentiated paragraph and then roughly two-thirds blank page — and those are precisely the three deliverables the brief asked for: what to build first, what to estimate, what the report cannot say. The p.5 sequencing argument names Priority one/two/three inside running prose instead of a numbered build order; p.6 lists the estimation approach for Scope 3 categories as a single block with no per-category table; p.7's "will not be able to say" content is a paragraph rather than an explicit list an audit committee can sign against. The result is a rhythm break — pages 2–4 fill the column, pages 5–8 fill a quarter of it — that makes the back half look like an afterthought. Not shippable unchanged for that reason alone. On genericness: the artefact is clearly built for this brief — the ESRS E/S/G pillar split, the fifteen-category Scope 3 definition box, the 19-datapoint estimation policy and the "provisional rather than final" framing could not be dropped into another document — though the visual language (single blue accent, hairline rules, plain bar chart) is conventional corporate reporting.

Integrity is largely intact — no clipped text or placeholder strings visible, and the page-3 readiness table and page-4 KPI row (82 / 34 / 29 / 19 with labels) render fully. But the document fails badly at the coherence level and even strains legibility. Pages 5, 6 and 7 each carry a single heading plus two or three short paragraphs and then roughly two-thirds of blank page below the text block; page 5 ('What to estimate, and how to disclose it honestly') is three paragraphs occupying the top quarter and nothing else, and page 7 ends with a two-item note and a lone source line, leaving the bottom 60% empty. That is not a rhythm, it is content that ran out — and it makes the back half of the deck read as unfinished next to the dense, well-built pages 2-4. Page 1 is also weakly composed: the title block sits mid-page with a thin rule above it and vast empty space above and below, no visual anchor, no device that recurs anywhere else in the document. Legibility is marginal in the page-3 table, whose four columns ('Readiness tier / Count / Share / Example datapoints / Recommended action' — five, in fact) are squeezed into the same measure as the body text, forcing the example-datapoint cells to wrap to three and four lines at a size noticeably smaller than the surrounding prose. Communicatively, the strongest work is real: the page-2 'Key takeaways' bullets and the page-3 tier table with counts and shares do the analytical job, and the page-4 KPI strip carries a source line. But no page contains a chart, and the 82/34/29/19 split — the entire spine of the brief — is never shown graphically, only tabulated and then repeated as numerals. Titles are decent ('What the first report will honestly not be able to say' is genuinely a conclusion, not a label), which is the one place this rises above boilerplate. On genericness: apart from the single accent rule under the title and the KPI numerals, nothing here is specific to a CSRD readiness assessment or to an audit-committee audience — swap the words and this is any consulting memo template. I would not send it with my name on it; pages 5-7 alone would need rebuilding.

Integrity holds: no clipping, overlap, or placeholder text on any of the eight pages, and the running header/footer ("CSRD Readiness Assessment" / "Confidential — Committee use only" / page x of 8 / date) is intact throughout. Legibility is acceptable, with an obvious single-column reading order. Coherence is genuinely consistent — every section page uses the same title-plus-rule treatment, the same left-set measure, and the same bordered aside pattern ("Key takeaways" p2, "Method note" p3, "Disclosure principle" p6, "Why say this" p7). It fails at communicative effectiveness. Page 3, "Where the 82 datapoints stand today," is the page that exists to carry the 34 / 29 / 19 split against 82 and it is delivered entirely as three prose paragraphs — no table, no bar, nothing a committee can scan or take away. Page 5, "What to build first," encodes a sequenced roadmap as "First... Second... Third..." inside one dense paragraph rather than as an ordered structure with owners and dates, despite the text itself naming owners and target dates. The only quantified display in the document is the stat row on page 4 (0% / 15 / 2–3), and one of those three, "2–3 Categories prioritised first," is a recommendation dressed as a measurement. Density also collapses in the back half: pages 5, 6 and 7 each carry roughly a third of a page of text with the remaining two-thirds blank, and page 8's "Recommendation" — the page the audit committee will actually act on — is three short paragraphs floating above a mostly empty sheet. The cover is similarly thin: a rule, title, subtitle and date in the top quarter with nothing below. On genericness, the writing is clearly built for this brief (the page-7 title "What the first report will honestly not be able to say" and the page-4 "Scope 3 is the material gap" are conclusions, not labels), but the visual system is an interchangeable corporate report shell — thin blue rule, sans headings, boxed asides — that would look identical under any other title.

Integrity holds: no clipping, no placeholder text, no overlap on any of the five pages; the header/footer chrome ("Nordic Market Entry Assessment" / section label top, "Confidential — Board Use Only", page x/5, September 2026 bottom) repeats identically on pages 2–5. Legibility is fine — dark type on white, obvious single-column reading order, headings clearly above body. Coherence passes too: the blue rule under each page title, the blue-rule-bounded pull box on page 2, the bulleted 'Key takeaways' block, and the callout treatment on page 3 ('Market sizing') all follow the same grid and colour, and nothing reads as hand-placed. It stops at level 3 on communicative effectiveness for two reasons. First, density: page 3 fills roughly the top 45% of the sheet, page 4 the top 40%, and page 5 the top 45% — three consecutive pages of half-empty paper in a five-page board document, which makes the deck feel padded rather than deliberately airy. Second, the brief asked to show payback under both cases and page 4 shows it only as three inline stat figures (2.1€m / 26mo / 34mo) plus two paragraphs of prose; there is no timeline, table or chart anywhere in the document contrasting base and pessimistic payback, and no visual of the EUR 340m / 9% market either. Credit where due: page titles are conclusions not labels ('Two incumbents hold 61% share but no Finnish product', 'The investment pays back within three years either way'), the stat figures carry units and sub-labels, and both the internal financial model source line under page 4's stats and the 'Notes and sources' list on page 5 are present. On genericness: the wording is specific to this brief, but the artefact itself — blue hairline under a sans heading, running head, plain single column of body text — would look identical for any consulting memo with different words dropped in; nothing about the layout is derived from this market-entry decision.

Integrity holds: no clipping, no placeholder text, no overlaps; the cover (p1), the KPI row on p4 (340 €m / 9% / 61% with 'Nordic market size', 'Annual growth rate', 'Incumbent combined share' captions and a source line), the payback table on p5 (Base case 2.1m / month 26 / '—'; Pessimistic 2.1m / month 34 / '+8 months') and the risks list on p7 all render what was intended. Coherence is also solid: the header rule with 'Nordic Market Entry' left and the section label right ('Recommendation', 'Market', 'Competitive', 'Payback', 'Conditions', 'Risks'), the footer 'Confidential — Board / x/7 / 8 September 2026', and the blue rule under each H1 repeat identically on pp2–7; the 'Method' callout on p3 and the 'Notes and sources' block on p7 use the same left-rule treatment. Where it fails is level 4. Every content page is roughly one-third full: p2 ends at about 45% of the page, p3 at 33%, p4 at 40%, p5 at 42%, p6 at 30%, p7 at 33% — six consecutive pages with a blank lower two-thirds, which reads as one-idea-per-page padding rather than a board document. There is no chart anywhere; the brief's 'show the payback under both cases' is served only by a four-row table on p5, with no visual of the 26 vs 34 month curve or the EUR 2.1m spend profile, and p6's three entry conditions are a bare numbered list where the page had room for a structured condition/owner/test treatment. Small artefact: a stray two-character glyph sits under the header rule at the left on pp2–7, above each H1. Genericness is mid: the content is unmistakably this brief (Finnish-language gap, Stockholm office, month-26 breakeven), and the KPI row and source lines show intent, but the visual system — single blue accent, one heading weight, plain table, all-left-aligned single column — would look identical for any other assessment.

Integrity holds: no clipping, no placeholder text, the page-3 bar chart, page-4 comparison table and page-2 KPI row all render, and the header/footer pair (section name right, 'Board Confidential / x/5 / September 2026') repeats identically on pages 2-5. Legibility is fine — body copy is a normal report size, the blue-on-white accents and rules carry contrast, and reading order is unambiguous. Coherence is solid: the same blue hairline under each H1, the same eyebrow/heading/lede stack, consistent table and callout treatment on page 4.

It stops at level 3 on communicative effectiveness. (a) Every page title is a filing label, not a conclusion — 'Market Opportunity', 'Financial Case', 'Conditions for Entry' would sit on any assessment; the page-3 title should say the Finnish gap is the wedge, the page-4 title should say the base case pays back in 26 months. (b) The page-3 chart is badly scaled: the y-axis runs to 800 while the three bars sit at ~340-400, so half the plot area is empty and the 9% CAGR the page is arguing for reads as flat — the chart actively undercuts its own takeaway line. (c) The brief asked to show payback under both cases; payback exists only as two numbers in the page-4 table ('Breakeven (month) 26.0 / 34.0'), with no cumulative-cash-flow curve, and the months are formatted to one decimal ('18.0', '26.0', '34.0'), which reads as a spreadsheet dump rather than a board figure. (d) Density is uneven: pages 2, 4 and 5 all stop around the halfway mark of the sheet, leaving large dead lower halves — page 4 in particular ends just after a three-row table and a one-sentence assumption box, which does not justify a full page.

Genericness is moderate rather than high: the argument is specific (the Finnish-language localization wedge, the 61% fragmented incumbent share, the month-26 vs month-34 spread, the three named conditions on page 5 with a twelve-month checkpoint), but the shell around it — blue rule, eyebrow, three-KPI band, figure caption, 'Notes and sources' numbered list — is the standard consulting chassis and would look identical for any other market-entry brief.

Integrity holds: no clipping, overlap or placeholder text anywhere; the page-3 column chart, the page-4 depot-capacity table and the page-2 stat row (31% / 12-41 / 8.2€m) all render fully. Legibility is acceptable for a printed report, though the page-4 table footnote and the page-3 figure caption sit at the small end and the page-4 'Definition' sidebar is the lightest text on the sheet. Visual coherence is the document's real strength: the thin blue rule under every H1, the running header (document title left, section right), the 'Confidential' footer with page x/8 and date, and the source line under both the chart and the table repeat identically across pages 2-8, and the accent blue of the chart bars matches the title-page rule and the stat figures. It fails at level 4 on density and completeness. Pages 5, 6, 7 and 8 each use only the top third to two-fifths of the page: page 5 'Recommended Sequencing' is a single unbroken paragraph over about 60% blank page, and page 8 'Recommendation' is one paragraph plus a two-item Notes list, leaving the rest empty — the document reads as four full pages followed by four stubs. Page 6 is the worst content failure: the brief asked for the six-month milestones and the page titled 'Six-Month Milestones' names only two (month 3 and month 6), leaving the intervening cadence unstated and most of the page white. Titles are also descriptive rather than conclusive — 'Cost of Deferring the Dispatch Migration' (p7) and 'Recommended Sequencing' (p5) name the topic but not the finding, where the page-7 body actually concludes a EUR 1.1m contingent cost. Page 3 is the one page that does this right: the caption carries a takeaway (EUR 3.3m of synergy is unreachable without one dispatch system) plus a source line. Genericness: the numbers are the brief's, but the shell — centred blue-ruled title block on a near-empty page 1, one stat triplet, one blue bar chart, one bordered table — is a stock consulting-report frame that would look identical for any acquisition brief.

Integrity mostly holds — no clipping or placeholder text visible — but page 7 is the failure: the 'Recommendation to the Steering Committee' page carries three short numbered approvals plus a two-item 'Notes and sources' list and then roughly two-thirds of blank page below, and the document simply stops there. Page 5 has the same problem (milestone table ends around a third down, then dead space), and page 6 leaves half a page empty under 'Cost of Deferring the Dispatch Migration'. That is not deliberate white space; it is the same one-block-per-page rhythm running out of content. Legibility is fine: the body text, the Key takeaways bullets on page 2 and the KPI band (31%, 12/41, 8.2 EUR m) read clearly, and reading order is unambiguous. Coherence is where it stalls short of level 3: the running header/footer repeat correctly, but the pages have wildly inconsistent vertical mass — page 3 is a full column of text plus chart, pages 5-7 are top-anchored fragments — so the grid does not hold across the set. The single chart on page 3 is a two-bar column chart (system-dependent vs dispatch-dependent) that is mostly empty plot area for two numbers a sentence could carry, and its axis label 'Annual synergy (EUR m)' is the only place the unit lives. Titles are competent and conclusive in places ('Cost of Deferring the Dispatch Migration', 'Overlap and Synergy Baseline') but page 4's 'Recommended Integration Sequence' and page 7's 'Recommendation to the Steering Committee' are labels, not conclusions — neither states the recommendation in the title. Genericness: the blue rule under the title, the three-up KPI strip, the small-caps section eyebrow and the plain two-column tables are a recognisable report shell; swap the words and this is any integration deck. Nothing about the composition responds to the specific tension in the brief (unbudgeted migration vs shrinking 40% synergy) except in prose. Not something I would send to a steering committee with my name on it while three of seven pages are half empty.

Integrity holds: no clipping, no placeholder text, and the repeated header ("Post-Acquisition Integration Assessment" with right-hand section tag) and three-part footer ("Confidential — Steering Committee Only" / page x of 5 / date) run consistently on pages 2–5. Legibility is fine at print size. Coherence is also held: one blue accent rule under the cover title and under the "Key takeaways" head on page 2, one heading weight, one body size, and the callout box on page 3 ("Synergy dividend") is styled the same as the notes block on page 5. Where it stops is level 4. Every page ends between 40% and 60% down the sheet — page 2 stops after two short paragraphs, page 3 after the second body block, page 4 after the milestone paragraph — so the document reads as four half-pages rather than a paced argument, and the whitespace is dead, not structural. Page 4 is the specific failure: the three numerals 1–6 / 7–12 / 13–18 with their one-line captions are a good device, but the actual six-month milestones the brief asked for are dumped underneath as a single unbroken ~10-line paragraph ("Months 1 to 6: consolidate all 12 overlapping depots... Months 7 to 12... Months 13 to 18..."), which both duplicates and buries the structure the numerals promised — those should be three columns of bullets under the numerals they belong to. There is also no table or chart anywhere: 12 of 41 depots, 31% customer overlap, and the 60/40 split of EUR 8.2m are all carried in prose on page 3, where a single split-bar or a depot table would have done more work than the paragraph. Titles are genuinely conclusive ("Deferral Costs More Than a Year of Savings", "Overlap Delivers Fast Wins; System Migration Unlocks the Rest"), units are attached, and page 5 carries a numbered source — those are the strong parts. Genericness is middling: the assertive titles and the phase numerals are specific to this brief, but the visual system (one blue rule, one accent colour, no exhibit) is a stock consulting-report shell that would look identical for any other assessment.

Integrity holds: no clipping, overlap or placeholder text anywhere — page 3's chart, page 4's five-column tier table and page 5's numbered sources all render complete. Legibility is fine; body copy, the 12%/40%/34% KPI numerals on page 2 and the table cells on page 4 all read at document size, and the reading order down each page is unambiguous.
